common_name: Claire Austin Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and support for training, since Claire Austin is vigorous enough to be grown as a short climber or kept pruned as a large shrub.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing support if training the vigorous canes upright as a short climber. Introduced by David Austin in 2007 and named for his daughter-in-law, Claire Austin carries large, cupped, pale creamy-white to soft lemon blooms that fade toward pure white as they open, with a strong myrrh fragrance that intensifies on warm days. Its vigorous, somewhat lax growth habit allows it to be trained against a fence or pillar for extra height, or kept as a large freestanding shrub with regular pruning, and it repeat-blooms well from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: James Galway Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; James Galway's arching, vigorous canes can be trained as a short climber or left to form a large, rounded shrub.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, or train the more vigorous stems upward for extra height. Introduced by David Austin in 2005 and named for the celebrated flutist, James Galway produces large, full, rounded rosette flowers in a soft, warm pink with a strong old-rose fragrance carrying hints of myrrh, held on sturdy, slightly arching canes clothed in glossy, disease-resistant foliage. It repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost and its vigorous, adaptable habit suits both a mixed border and, with support, a short climbing position on a fence or trellis.

common_name: Jude the Obscure Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Jude the Obscure's large, heavy flowers benefit from a bit of afternoon shade in the hottest climates to extend their bloom life.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1995, Jude the Obscure carries large, deeply cupped, golden-yellow blooms that pale toward the outer petals as they mature, famous for one of the strongest and most distinctive fragrances of any English rose, a rich, fruity scent often described as fresh guava. Its full, heavy flowers can nod on their stems, especially after rain, and it is a somewhat lax, medium-sized shrub best sited where its fragrance can be enjoyed up close, repeat-blooming from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Crocus Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Crocus Rose's compact, well-branched habit and strong disease resistance make it a forgiving choice for gardeners newer to English roses.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2000, Crocus Rose bears soft apricot-yellow buds that open into rounded, rosette-shaped flowers fading gracefully to a warm buff-cream, carrying a light, sweet tea fragrance on a compact, bushy, disease-resistant shrub. Its manageable size and reliably healthy foliage make it well suited to a smaller border or foundation planting, and it repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Queen of Sweden Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Queen of Sweden's upright, narrow growth habit fits a tighter space in the border than the more sprawling English rose cultivars.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2004, Queen of Sweden bears soft, pure pink, cupped rosette flowers with a light myrrh fragrance on an upright, narrow, well-branched shrub that stays notably tidy and self-supporting compared to more lax English rose cultivars. It is among the most disease-resistant of the David Austin roses, holding clean, healthy foliage through humid summers with minimal spraying, and it repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost, making it a reliable choice for a narrow bed or formal border planting.
